claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
The baseline alloy has high density and insufficient room-temperature ductility.
Adding 1-3 at.% Si is sufficient to exceed the solubility limit of Si in the BCC matrix.
Minor Si addition will precipitate a secondary intermetallic silicide phase.
The secondary phase may be (Ti,Zr)5Si3 or a similar silicide.
The silicide will form a continuous or semi-continuous reticulated network at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
The reticulated intermetallic network will force propagating cracks to deflect and branch.
Crack deflection and branching will increase fracture-surface area and dissipate energy.
The proposed network mechanism will mitigate catastrophic brittle failure and increase room-temperature compressive ductility.
Si addition will produce a slight increase in yield strength relative to the baseline alloy.
The density change caused by Si addition will be negligible or slightly positive and less than 1%.
Si has an atomic weight of approximately 28.
The proposed density increase could result from Si replacing lighter elements or occupying interstitial sites.
Solid-solution hardening primarily increases yield strength and often reduces ductility.
A beneficial response requires a Si concentration that creates a continuous network without producing large isolated brittle inclusions.
Large isolated silicide inclusions would act as critical flaws.
At high temperature, the silicides may coarsen or dissolve, so the proposed behavior may not extend to creep conditions.
The prediction is specifically intended for room-temperature uniaxial compression.
